steps.goal: Write the overview: 4 KiB, 32-byte lines, 128 lines. Show the 32-bit byte-address split into tag[31:12] (20 bits), index[11:5] (7 bits), word[4:2] and byte[1:0]. Define the parameters and mark which are fixed by the spec and which may be generalised.

options: write-back + write-allocate
write-through + no-allocate
decisions.choice: Write-back with write-allocate. A store miss always refills the line before merging.
decisions.rationale: P3 states this explicitly. The bus also forces it: the write-data channel has no byte strobes and only full-line bursts exist.

steps.title: Define the CPU request/response port and the interconnect burst port signal by signal
steps.goal:
Specify both external interfaces with widths, directions and handshake rules.
- CPU side: req valid/ready carrying addr, we, wdata and wstrb; a single resp_valid with rdata; responses in order with no ID; no uncached bit.
- Bus side: request channel (line-aligned addr, rw, valid/ready); write-data channel (valid/ready/last, no strobes); read-data channel (valid/last, no ready); write-done pulse.
- Protocol consequences: no error signalling, read data must always be sunk, no partial-line writes.
- There is no maintenance sideband port.

spec_evidence.quote: On the CPU side, the core issues one request at a time using a valid/ready handshake
(address, read/write, write data, byte strobes)
per hit. Responses come back in order on a single response-valid strobe. The core always
waits for each response, so you don't need an ID.
channel (line-aligned address, read/write) with valid/ready, a write-data channel with
valid/ready/last, a read-data channel with valid/last (the cache must always accept read
data, so there's no ready), and a write-done pulse when a write burst is committed. Bursts
are always one full line, 8 beats of 32 bits, in incrementing order starting at word 0.

done_when: Every port is listed in a table with name, direction, width and description
Handshake rules are stated: a transfer occurs on valid&&ready, and the payload is held stable while valid&&!ready

Interface notes record whether wstrb is ignored on loads

steps.title: Lay out storage: data SRAM, tag SRAM, valid/dirty flop arrays and victim line buffer
steps.goal: Map the 4 KiB of data and the 128 tags onto single-port, 1-cycle synchronous SRAMs with byte enables. Keep valid and dirty in flops so that reset clears them in one cycle. Size the victim line buffer needed for evictions. Draw the top-level block diagram connecting the arrays, the lookup stage, the miss FSM and the two ports.

spec_evidence.quote: The physical design team says we get single-port synchronous SRAMs with 1-cycle read
latency and byte-write enables. They would rather keep valid/dirty out of SRAM so a reset
doesn't take 128 cycles.

options: 1024x32 word-wide single-port SRAM with 4 byte enables
128x256 line-wide SRAM with 32 byte enables
8 banks of 128x32
decisions.choice: One 1024x32 single-port data SRAM addressed by {index,word} with 4 byte-write enables, plus a separate 128x20 single-port tag SRAM.
decisions.rationale: This matches both the 32-bit CPU access and the 32-bit bus beat. Refill writes and writeback reads move one word per cycle with no wide muxing, and the byte enables serve store strobes directly.
decisions.question: Is a single 1024x32 data SRAM plus a 128x20 tag SRAM an acceptable macro configuration, or does physical design need specific SRAM shapes or banking?

options: 128-entry valid and dirty flop arrays
valid/dirty bits in tag SRAM
decisions.choice: Valid and dirty live in two 128-bit flop arrays that reset clears. The tag SRAM is not initialised.
decisions.rationale: P6 asks to keep valid/dirty out of SRAM so that reset does not take 128 cycles.

done_when: Block diagram shows the CPU port, lookup/compare stage, data SRAM, tag SRAM, valid/dirty flops, victim buffer, miss FSM and bus port, with no maintenance or uncached path
Each array has its depth, width, port type and address source listed
The read and write uses of each SRAM port are enumerated per operation: load hit, store hit, refill and writeback

steps.title: Design the 1-cycle load-hit pipeline that accepts a request every cycle
steps.goal: Define the two-stage flow. In the accept cycle, the CPU address drives the tag and data SRAM reads. In the next cycle, the tag compare and valid check produce resp_valid and rdata. Work out how req_ready is generated so back-to-back read hits run at full rate without a combinational path from SRAM output to ready. Define what happens to a younger request that was already accepted when the older one misses.

spec_evidence.quote: (address, read/write, write data, byte strobes). We'd like hits to return data the cycle
after the request is accepted, with a new request accepted every cycle for back-to-back
On the CPU side, the core issues one request at a time using a valid/ready handshake

options: Speculatively accept the next request; on a miss in stage 1, hold it in a replay register and re-read the SRAMs after the miss
Gate req_ready combinationally on the stage-1 hit result
decisions.choice: Speculative accept with a one-entry replay holding register. req_ready depends only on registered state (FSM idle, stage-1 not a store), never on the tag compare.
decisions.rationale: This keeps the SRAM-to-compare-to-ready-to-core path off the critical path while still giving full-rate read hits. At most one younger request can be in flight.
decisions.question: While a load's hit/miss is being resolved, may the cache already have accepted the next request (and replay it later), or must req_ready only rise once the previous access is known to hit?

done_when: Stage diagram shows what happens in the accept cycle and in the response cycle of a load hit
The req_ready equation uses only registered signals
The replay path is defined: the younger request is held, and its SRAM read is redone after the miss completes
A waveform shows 4 back-to-back load hits with one response per cycle

steps.title: Design the store-hit path within the 2-cycle budget on single-port SRAM
steps.goal:
A store needs the tag compare (from an SRAM read) before its byte-enabled data write, and the data SRAM has only one port. Define:
- when the write happens,
- how the next request is held off,
- when the store response is returned,
- when the dirty bit is set.
Show that loads following stores see the correct data.

options: 2-cycle store: read tag in cycle 1, compare and byte-write data SRAM in cycle 2, req_ready low for that cycle
Store buffer: write deferred into a free SRAM cycle, with load forwarding
decisions.choice: 2-cycle store with no store buffer. The data SRAM byte-write happens in the compare cycle, and the response is issued in that same cycle. req_ready is deasserted during that cycle, so stores sustain one every 2 cycles.
decisions.rationale: This meets the stated limit of 2 cycles per store hit. It avoids a store buffer and its forwarding and hazard logic.
decisions.question: Is a store-hit throughput of one store every 2 cycles (no store buffer) acceptable, or should back-to-back stores sustain one per cycle?

decisions.topic: Dirty eviction structure and ordering vs. refill
options: Copy victim into an 8x32 victim buffer, then issue the refill read and drain the writeback in parallel
Serial: write back the victim, wait for write-done, then issue the refill read
Read the victim directly from the SRAM into the write channel with a skid register
decisions.choice: 8-word victim buffer. Copy the victim out of the SRAM (8 cycles), issue the refill read request, and send the writeback burst from the buffer in parallel. Any later miss that needs the victim buffer, or that reads the victim's line address, waits for write-done of the outstanding writeback.
decisions.rationale: This takes the writeback off the critical refill path on a 10–20 cycle bus. Using write-done as the commit point preserves read-after-write ordering on the shared interconnect without assuming the channels are ordered.
decisions.question: Does the interconnect guarantee that a read issued after a write burst to the same line returns the new data, or must the cache wait for write-done before reading it back? Is a parallel writeback and refill with an 8-word victim buffer acceptable?

options: Refill the line, then replay the store through the normal store-hit path
Merge store bytes into the matching refill beat as it is written
decisions.choice: Refill the whole line, then replay the original request (load or store) through the lookup pipeline. The response comes from the replayed hit.
decisions.rationale: This reuses the hit datapath and keeps a single response source. The cost is 1–2 extra cycles per miss.
decisions.question: Is it acceptable for a miss to complete by replaying the access as a hit after the refill (1–2 extra cycles), rather than forwarding or merging data during the refill?

options: None: respond after the full line is refilled
Early restart: forward the requested word as its beat arrives (bus order is fixed from word 0)
Critical-word-first (not possible: bursts always start at word 0)
decisions.choice: No critical-word-first, because the bus cannot reorder beats, and no early restart. The response is returned after all 8 beats are written and the access is replayed.
decisions.rationale: P5 fixes burst order starting at word 0, so true CWF would need interconnect changes. Early restart adds forwarding and hazard logic that a first cut does not need.
decisions.question: Since bursts always start at word 0, critical-word-first is not possible. Do you want early restart (return the requested word as soon as its beat arrives), or is waiting for the full line acceptable for the first cut?

steps.title: Document the agreed scope: no uncached/MMIO path and no cache maintenance in this version
steps.goal:
Record the user-confirmed answers to the P7 open items. The cache has no uncached path; the core or a wrapper must decode MMIO and route it around the cache. The cache has no flush or invalidate of any kind. State the architectural consequences:
- an MMIO-addressed request reaching the cache is cached like any other;
- DMA coherence is not maintained by the cache, so dirty data reaches memory only on natural eviction.
List the proposed follow-ups as non-implemented hooks: a flush_req/inv_req sideband walking 128 indices, and a cpu_req_uncached bit with single-beat bus transactions. Note which structures already make them cheap, such as the flop-based valid/dirty and the reusable writeback path.

spec_evidence.quote: Things we haven't decided yet: cache maintenance ops (flush/invalidate), uncached regions
for MMIO, and whether to do critical-word-first. Make a call and tell us what you assumed.
We looked at write-through, but the bus is shared with the DMA and the

options: No uncached path: all accesses through this port are cacheable, and MMIO is routed around the cache by the core/SoC
Parameterised uncached address window using full-line bursts
Add a separate single-beat uncached bus port
decisions.choice: No uncached path. Every CPU-port request is cached, and the core or a wrapper must decode MMIO ranges and route them around the cache. A cpu_req_uncached bit with single-beat transactions is only a possible future option and would need an interconnect protocol extension.
decisions.rationale: Settled by the user's answer to Q1.

options: Sideband maintenance port with whole-cache clean+invalidate (flush) and invalidate-all
Per-address clean/invalidate encoded as extra CPU request types
No maintenance ops
decisions.choice: No maintenance ops and no invalidate path in this version. A flush_req/inv_req sideband walking all 128 indices is only a proposed follow-up.
decisions.rationale: Settled by the user's answer to Q2.

steps.title: Specify the single clock domain and reset behaviour of flop state vs. SRAM contents
steps.goal: Document the one clock shared by the core, the cache and the interconnect. Define the reset style and which state is reset: valid/dirty arrays, FSM, handshake outputs, victim buffer and replay register. Make sure the tag and data SRAMs need no initialisation, as the PD team asked. Note that reset is the only way to invalidate the cache in this version.

spec_evidence.quote: latency and byte-write enables. They would rather keep valid/dirty out of SRAM so a reset
doesn't take 128 cycles.

options: Single clock, synchronous active-low reset
Single clock, asynchronous-assert/synchronous-deassert reset
Separate core and bus clocks with CDC
decisions.choice: The cache, core and interconnect share a single clock. Reset is active-low, asserted asynchronously and deasserted synchronously. The valid/dirty arrays and all control and handshake flops are reset; SRAM contents and datapath registers are not.
decisions.rationale: The spec mentions no second clock. Async-assert/sync-deassert is common practice for microcontroller blocks, and it keeps reset to one cycle as P6 wants.
decisions.question: Do the core and the system interconnect run on the same clock as the D-cache? What reset convention (sync/async, polarity) does Kestrel use?

done_when: The clock and reset ports are defined, with reset polarity and synchronisation

The MA notes that reset discards dirty data without writeback, because no flush exists
